questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I have Korean heritage, so I wanted to be closer to my family, experience living in Korea and improve my Korean language skills. Exchange is a good opportunity to experience living in a different country/city without the uncertainty and commitment that studying/working there full time would bring.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I could find what I needed, but sometimes you had to dig far into emails or go through a series of weblinks to find what you were looking for. But generally Ewha was good at giving you the information you needed (I'd recommend saving the files somewhere or writing down important information so you don't have to spend a lot of time finding the information again)

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I didn't need any assistance.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Dorm rooms, single and two-person, but it wasn't possible to choose.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: There was a kitchen in a different building (and you have to buy all your own equipment, but it's cheap) and a small kitchenette on each floor with a microwave and a sink. I didn't cook at all because it's pretty cheap to eat out! There's also a cafeteria + restaurant + cafe in the dorms (open on weekdays only) with 1,000KRW breakfast, ~6,000KRW lunch and ~10,000KRW dinner. Generally you can get dinner for 10,000KRW outside of campus as well.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
You should be okay with living with a roommate if you choose to live in the dorms. It obviously depends on who you get as a roommate (Ewha doesn't do any survey to match roommates) so it can be a bit hit or miss, but I find it bearable since it's only for a couple of months and I can just sit at the library or in a cafe if I get tired of being in the dorms. 
In the dorm they have study rooms in the basement (very bare bones), a laundry room and a small fitness room (limited equipment and weights). The rooms each have their own bathroom, but the whole wall towards the room is glass so there's no sound isolation, but you get used to it.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The registration period is after you arrive (in the dorms at least), the week right before the semester starts. They say competition is tough and a lot of people couldn't get all the courses they wanted, but I got what I wanted and didn't have any issues. You can choose more courses than you need and drop them afterwards. The week before you can access the portal without being able to register, where you can see the capacity for each course

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: They sent an email outlining the process beforehand

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very, I got all of the ones I wanted + backups

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I'd recommend having a list of course codes ready to copy paste and make sure to check that the schedule fits and have backup courses ready in case you don't get what you wanted. And be ready at your computer when registration opens! (Also some courses are available in both English and Korea, with different course codes, so make sure you choose the right one)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took a mix of easy and more difficult courses

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: They don't have anything like øvelsestimer, it's all just lectures, generally each 1:15 hrs two times a week. So anything practical like solving problems etc. aren't really part of the teaching, you have to do that yourself. Some of my courses (in computer science) had 'lab' sessions, but they would just explain some code and that was it.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Machine Learning, Graph Neural Networks, C programming and Lab, Human-Computer Interaction and Practical Korean 301

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I'd generally recommend taking a Korean language course if you're interested and your degree allows it (you have to go to the Korean version of the course catalogue to find them - Ewha also sends an email about it before registration opens. You can get Korean courses that are either 3 or 6 credits). If you want a chill exchange, I'd recommend taking Ceramics and generally taking courses made for exchange students because they're more lax. Anything that is a major requirement or generally has more Korean students, seem to grade on a scale whereas ones for exchange students seem to give absolute grades. I would also recommend C programming.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I can't think of any, but I will caveat my lack of insurance expenses by the fact that I still fall under my parent's insurance and I also have Korean citizenship, so I don't need to pay for Korean health insurance either. (Ewha requires that you have both a private insurance from home and that you pay for the Korean national health insurance). Also 4/5 of my classes didn't require any textbooks, but I also mainly took Computer Science classes (It was only Korean that required textbooks)

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Transportation is really cheap and generally you can get most things you need in walking distance, I only travel around Seoul for the sake of seeing Seoul. (And there are a lot of things to do near Ewha!)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: They have clubs and it's possible to join them as an exchange student, but they don't really advertise them, so you have to find the club's instagram pages to see how/when to join. Typically you can join them in the first week of the semester. They have a couple of sports you can join through the gym, though.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Fitness center, sports, clubs and cultural exchange clubs

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I joined Hangeul Assi, which paired you with a mentor you could practice Korean with, which was quite nice! They also have various other similar clubs. In general I would recommend to sign up immediately to things because there's often tough competition!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: It's easy to find recommendations for cultural attractions, cafes, shops and weekend trips, so if I were to recommend something else, I would recommend checking out craft workshops in Seoul, if that's something you're interested in. They have so many different types (leatherwork, mother of pearl lacquerware, bookbinding, screenprinting, ceramics, painting, tufting, you name it) and they all have one-day classes, but some also have ones that go over multiple weeks. I only did one-day classes, and near Ewha I would recommend danchoodan (traditional korean bookbinding) and neote leather craft (right in front of Ewha!). It's a good way to make a souvenir and maybe even practice your Korean! I would also recommend taking dance classes since Korea is so known for it, there's e.g. JustJerk right in front of Ewha. (I would also like to shout out the craft museum in Seoul, it's my favourite museum of the ones I've been to in Seoul)

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy since I'm used to Korean culture

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: It's hard because you only have lectures and no one talks to each other, I'd say clubs are the best way to go

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I'm not sure

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Everything is open quite late and it's so normal to eat out alone

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Make a list of things you definitely want to do when you're on exchange and make sure you make plans for them because time will fly by and you don't want to regret not getting to do the things you wanted to do! 
2) It's okay if you don't make lifelong friends and it's completely okay to do things alone, don't compare yourself to other people's instagram stories! (And you don't have to go to a new country every weekend!)
3) Take easy courses if you can
(Bonus: Make sure to go outside of campus and see the rest of Seoul! It can be easy to just stay on campus because you have everything you need there)

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I can't think of anything

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Being more comfortable doing things alone, honestly

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: My social battery was always low because I was sharing a room with someone and you have to be very proactive when it comes to making plans with people (because you don't naturally make friends in classes because they're lecture based). (Don't be afraid to reach out to people and don't be afraid to just do things alone!) Ewha was also not the best at making events etc. for meeting other exchange students, it was very do-it-yourself.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
